 Will a power station run a 30 amp RV?
 A power station with a TT-30R outlet can power a 30 amp RV up to the station’s own AC output, not up to the 3,600W the connection is rated for. TT-30 is the 120V, 30A plug and receptacle type on a typical 30 amp RV cord, and 120V × 30A = 3,600W. A connector rating is not available power. The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 has a TT-30R outlet but 2,400W of total AC output, about 20A at 120V (2,400W ÷ 120V, at a power factor of 1). Our van and weekend picks have no TT-30R outlet. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra Plus gives 3,600W in total across its AC outlets, the same figure as the TT-30 rating. EcoFlow’s US page lists up to 30A at its TT-30R outlet and up to 20A at each of its four other AC outlets, all within that 3,600W total. In TheSolarLab’s review (no date shown), the TT-30R outlet shut off first when the total went above 3,600W, even with the extra load on the 20A outlets, so keep the total under that limit when the RV runs from it.
 Among the models we track, the BLUETTI AC200L, Elite 300 and Apex 300, the EcoFlow DELTA Pro and DELTA 3 Ultra Plus, the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 and the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus list a TT-30R outlet. Before connecting an RV shore cord, have a qualified RV technician check the station, adapter and RV protection system together, including neutral and ground arrangements and any EMS or GFCI requirements. Do not bypass a protective-device warning or improvise a bonding modification. Before you plug in, switch off the air conditioner and other large loads, then add up what is left. Keep the total within our planning budget of 90% of the station’s continuous output: 2,160W on the C2000 Gen 2 (2,400W × 0.9) and 3,240W on the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus (3,600W × 0.9).
 Count the converter
 When the shore cord is plugged in, the RV’s converter turns 120V into 12V for the lights, the water pump and the fans, and it charges the house battery. A 55A converter such as the WFCO WF-8955 can put out about 790W at 14.4V (55A × 14.4V), and it draws more than that from the station because of conversion losses. If the house battery is low, that load starts as soon as you plug in, and part of the station’s energy goes into the house battery instead of your devices. If you want to disable house-battery charging, have the RV technician identify whether the converter has a dedicated breaker and confirm that the house battery can continue supplying the required DC loads and safety equipment. Do not switch off an unidentified circuit. Otherwise, count the converter in your total. The RV’s 12V loads also pass through two conversions this way, the station’s inverter and the converter, so they use more of the station’s energy than they would from its own 12V port.
 Do not charge the station from the RV while the RV runs from the station. A station plugged into an RV outlet, or into a 12V socket fed by the house battery, would charge itself from its own output through the converter, and each conversion loses energy.
 Air conditioner and microwave
 The rooftop air conditioner is often the largest load in an RV. Dometic’s installation manual lists 12.4A for the compressor and 2.5A for the fan on its 13,500 BTU Brisk II, 14.9A in total. At 115V that is about 1,714VA (14.9A × 115V). We plan with 1,714W, as if the power factor were 1, so actual watts may be lower. At start the compressor can draw 68A for a moment, and Dometic recommends a generator of at least 3.5kW for one unit. That is generator advice, not a rating for a battery station. A station’s continuous output does not show whether it starts this compressor, so check the start-up surge separately with the station maker and the air conditioner maker. A soft-start device can lower the start-up current, but treat it as a condition to confirm with both makers, not as a tested fix. If the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus starts the unit, it runs it at full load for about 1.5 hours by our calculation (3,072Wh × 0.85 ÷ 1,714W), longer while the compressor cycles off. These are examples, not compatibility tests.
 For a microwave, the input watts on the label count, not the cooking watts. Samsung lists 1,580W of input for its 1,000W ME16K3000 and 1,700W for its over-the-range ME19R7041FS. On the Elite 200 V2 , a 1,700W microwave leaves about 640W of our 2,340W planning budget (2,600W × 0.9) for anything else on its AC outlets. Five minutes at 1,700W use about 142Wh at the outlet (1,700W × 5 ÷ 60), about 167Wh of rated capacity at our 85% figure (142Wh ÷ 0.85). More in how many watts a microwave uses and its amps on 12V .

 50 amp RVs
 A 50 amp RV service has two 120V legs of 50A each, a connector rating of up to 12,000W (2 × 120V × 50A). That rating is not what a station supplies. A station feeds a 50 amp RV only up to its own output, and an adapter does not raise it. Ask the RV maker or a qualified RV technician which circuits can run from a station.
 How much power does a van use in a day?
 Our van day uses about 610Wh: a 12V compressor fridge, LED lights and a roof fan. It is the day all three picks had to cover, with a 20% allowance.
 12V fridge, about 300Wh. Dometic lists 0.98Ah per hour at 12V for its CFX3 35, with 90°F outside and 39°F inside. That is about 282Wh a day by our calculation (0.98Ah × 12V × 24 hours), and we plan with 300Wh.
 LED lights, 150Wh. 30W for 5 hours.
 Roof fan, 160Wh. 20W for 8 hours.

With our 20% allowance on the load energy, the calculated reference size under our assumptions is 862Wh rated (610Wh × 1.2 ÷ 0.85 = 861.2Wh, rounded up). For consistent screening, we apply an 85% delivered-energy assumption to this example. It is lower than our separate 92% DC assumption, but neither validates runtime for a particular station or wiring arrangement.
 The list leaves out phones, a laptop, cooking and heat. A laptop at 60W for 3 hours adds 180Wh. A coffee maker or an induction plate can draw more than 1,000W while it heats, so check its label. The size calculator adds up your own list.

The listed 10A outlet rating exceeds the cooler’s 7.5A rated DC current, but that comparison does not establish spare capacity for additional devices or verify startup. Check shared-output limits and the supplied cable.
 A bigger battery can cover a few cloudy days, but a daily shortfall still empties it. A van that uses 200Wh more than it takes in each day uses up 800Wh of stored energy in 4 days (200Wh × 4).  Can you charge a power station from the alternator?
 From a 12V car socket you can, but slowly. A DC-DC alternator charger wired to the vehicle battery can be several times faster and needs an installation.
 The C1000 Gen 2 supports car recharging with the specified cable, but do not use its 120W car-socket output rating to estimate charging speed. BLUETTI’s US manual (V2.0) lists the car socket input of the Elite 200 V2 at up to 96W from a 12V socket and up to 192W from a 24V socket. EcoFlow’s manual for the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus lists car charging into its solar input at 12V and 8A, about 96W. At 96W, a 4-hour drive adds about 384Wh before charging losses, less than one 610Wh van day.
 These alternator chargers come from the brands of our weekend and full-time picks. Available charging power depends on the charger settings, vehicle electrical system and installation. The advertised maximum does not establish spare alternator capacity.

 How does a power station connect to your RV's 12V system?
 There are two common ways: through the shore cord and the RV’s converter, or through a DC connection to the 12V side under the conditions below. The house battery runs the 12V side, which usually runs the lights, the water pump, the vent fans, the furnace fan and the fridge controls.
 Through the shore cord, the station supplies the RV circuits connected through the shore-power system, within the source and connection limits. That includes the converter that charges the house battery, as the TT-30 section above explains. On the 12V side, the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus has an Anderson port rated 12.6V and 30A, 378W in total shared with its car outlet, by EcoFlow’s US product page, an option for a properly designed connection. A regulated 12V output is not automatically a house-battery charger or a source that may be paralleled with the battery. Do not connect it directly to battery terminals or an energized RV DC bus unless the manufacturers support the arrangement and an RV technician designs the required protection and source isolation. On the C1000 Gen 2 and the Elite 200 V2 , plan the 12V car outlet, listed at 12V and 10A by each maker, for one 12V device such as a fridge, rather than for the RV’s 12V system.
 Use one path at a time. If the shore cord runs from the station, the converter already charges the house battery, so a second connection from the station’s 12V side adds conversion losses, not energy.
 Have a qualified RV technician make any connection to the RV’s wiring, with the right fuse and wire size.
 Can a power station run an RV absorption fridge?
 An absorption fridge can consume substantial battery energy on its electric heating element. If the manufacturer permits propane operation in the intended location and conditions, that mode can reduce electrical demand, while still requiring its specified 12V supply. These fridges, the 2-way and 3-way models in many trailers, cool with heat from a gas flame or an electric element. On 120V, the element heats whenever the fridge cools.
 On propane, the fridge still needs 12V for its controls. Norcold’s manual for its N611 and N811 lists a fault for when the DC voltage is too low to cool on propane. So keep the house battery charged, or supply that 12V from the station only through a connection that meets the conditions in the 12V system section . Our suggestion: while the fridge runs on propane, keep the RV’s CO alarm and LP gas detector working, and follow the fridge maker’s instructions for venting and service. Switch the fridge off propane while you refuel and wherever open flames are not allowed. A 12V compressor fridge such as the CFX3 35 is planned at about 300Wh a day in our van list. Our refrigerator picks and the refrigerator watts guide cover household fridges.
 Solar generator or gas generator for an RV?
 A fuel generator can resume operation after safe refueling, while a station must be recharged. A station runs without fuel or an engine at the campsite. Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide, so safety comes first. Run a generator outdoors only, far from doors, windows and vents, and turn it off and let it cool before you refuel, as the CPSC advises. Our suggestion for a campsite: point the exhaust away from your RV and other rigs, and keep the RV’s CO alarm working. Honda lists 48dB(A) at a quarter load and 57dB(A) at the 1,800W rated load for its EU2200i, without a measuring distance. National Park Service rules prohibit operation above 60dBA at 50ft and can also prohibit unreasonable noise below that level. Site-specific generator hours and other restrictions still apply. One 0.95 gallon tank runs the EU2200i for 3.2 hours at 1,800W, about 5,760Wh of AC output (1,800W × 3.2 hours), more than any of our three picks holds without extra batteries. This compares generator AC energy over one rated-load tank with battery storage capacity. It is not a like-for-like delivered-energy or cost comparison. A model is eligible when the configuration we price is in stock at the brand’s US store and its price was checked in the last 72 hours. Pre-orders, backorders, sold-out and discontinued models, and product pages without a way to order do not count. A model becomes eligible only after its PowerSized review is published. Minimums come first, then one number picks the winner, and a tie goes to the lower price.

 Questions buyers ask
 What size solar generator do I need for a 30 amp RV? Size it by your loads, not by the 30 amp plug. A TT-30 connection is rated for 3,600W (120V × 30A), but the station only has to cover what runs at the same time, within its own output. Add the watts of those devices for the output, and watts times hours for the capacity. For our list of a 12V fridge, lights and a fan, three days without sun give a calculated reference size under our assumptions of 2,584Wh rated (610Wh × 3 × 1.2 ÷ 0.85, rounded up), with our 20% allowance and our 85% delivered-energy assumption. It is not a validated minimum for every station and RV.
 How much solar do I need to run a 30 amp RV? Enough to put back what you use each day. With 5 equivalent peak-sun hours, 400W of supported panels deliver about 1,500Wh to the station's solar input (400W × 5 hours × 0.75), before charging losses, about 1,275Wh at your devices at our 85% figure. That is about twice our 610Wh van day. That example is not a budget for sustained rooftop-air-conditioner use. Estimate the air conditioner's energy separately from its operating watts and hours, and verify startup compatibility.
 Can you run an RV off a solar generator? For the 12V system, lights, fans, a fridge and short microwave use, often yes, if the station's output and capacity cover them. A rooftop air conditioner is harder. If the station starts it, a 3,600Wh station runs a 13,500 BTU unit for about 1.8 hours at full load by our calculation, under our illustrative 1,714W operating-load assumption, and the start-up surge has to be checked separately. Count the RV's converter too, which can charge the house battery from the station as soon as you plug in.
 How long will a 2000 watt solar generator run a refrigerator? The 2,000W rating is output, so look at its Wh. A 2,048Wh station gives about 1,741Wh at our 85% figure. A 12V compressor fridge planned at about 300Wh a day, like the Dometic CFX3 35 (about 282Wh a day at 90°F outside by our calculation from Dometic's figure), runs about 5.8 days on that (1,741 ÷ 300), without sun and before any allowance. An absorption fridge on its electric heating element can use far more. Propane mode, where its maker permits it, can reduce that demand and still needs its specified 12V supply.
 What can a 1000W portable power station run? A 1,000W rating tells you what can run at once, not for how long. In a van, it can run a 12V fridge, lights, a fan and phone charging when their total stays within its output and its 12V port's current limit. It does not run an RV microwave that draws 1,580 to 1,700W from the outlet, like the two Samsung models above. How long the rest runs depends on the station's Wh.
 What is the best power system for a camper van? For portable loads with compatible plug-in connections, a power station can avoid a built-in electrical installation. A hardwired roof fan or connection to the RV's DC system still requires the supported arrangement described in the 12V-system section. Under our assumptions, a station with a 12V outlet and panels can cover a 610Wh day of a fridge, lights and a fan like ours. A built-in system with a house battery, a DC-DC charger and a solar controller holds more but needs installation. Our van pick, the C1000 Gen 2 with 600W of solar input, fits the first case. Start from your daily Wh and how you charge between stops.

 RV Power Has Changed. Catch Up.
 RV and van life is booming. The RV Industry Association reported record shipment numbers heading into 2026, and the van life hashtag has over 15 million posts on Instagram alone. More people are living, working, and traveling on the road than ever before.
 And the single biggest quality-of-life upgrade for any RVer or van dweller? Reliable portable power that doesn't involve a noisy, smelly gas generator. 
 If you've ever boondocked on BLM land or camped at a Harvest Hosts property, you know the deal: there are no hookups. No shore power cord. No campground pedestal to plug into. You're on your own, and everything in your rig — the fridge, the lights, the water pump, the phone you're using to navigate tomorrow's route — needs power from somewhere.
 Gas generators technically work, but they're loud (often violating quiet-hours rules at campgrounds), they produce carbon monoxide, they vibrate the whole rig, and they need a supply of gasoline that takes up cargo space. Solar generators eliminate every one of those problems. Silent operation, zero emissions, no fuel to carry, and they recharge from panels mounted on your roof or set up at camp.
 But RV power demands are different from home backup or camping. You need units that handle road vibration, fit in limited cargo space, offer 12V compatibility, charge from the alternator while driving, and produce enough continuous output to run a residential fridge all day. Not every "best solar generator" qualifies.

With 200–400W of solar panels adding 800–1,600Wh back during the day, these units sustain multi-day boondocking comfortably.
 If you skip the TV and limit laptop use, you can cut daily consumption to 1,400–1,600Wh — within range of the Jackery 1000 Pro with supplemental solar.

 Buyer's Guide: Choosing the Right Solar Generator for Your RV
 RV use puts demands on a solar generator that home backup and casual camping don't. Here's what to prioritize when shopping for your setup.
 Weight vs. Capacity: The RV Tradeoff
 Every pound in an RV matters. Motorhomes have gross vehicle weight ratings (GVWR) that limit how much you can carry. Travel trailers have tongue weight and payload limits. Van builds are even more constrained — a Ram ProMaster 1500 has roughly 3,000 lbs of payload capacity, and a 75-pound power station eats a meaningful chunk of that.
 The Wh-per-pound ratio tells you how efficiently each unit converts weight into energy:
 ALLPOWERS R3500: 42.2 Wh/lb — most efficient for its class
 EcoFlow Delta 2 Max: 40.2 Wh/lb — excellent balance
 Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro: 39.4 Wh/lb — strong for a lighter unit
 BLUETTI AC200L: 33.0 Wh/lb — heavier chassis adds weight
 EcoFlow River 3 Plus: 18.6 Wh/lb — compact priority, not energy density
 For most RVers, the Delta 2 Max hits the sweet spot: enough capacity for a full day of moderate use, light enough to reposition if needed, and expandable for when you need more.
 Solar Panel Pairing for RV Roofs
 RV roofs are prime real estate for solar panels. Unlike portable panels that you set up and angle at camp, roof-mounted rigid panels charge passively — while you drive, while you sleep, while you're inside making lunch. For serious boondocking, roof solar is the single best upgrade you can make.
 Rigid Panels (Roof-Mounted)
 200W rigid panels bolt to the RV roof via Z-brackets or mounting rails. They're always working, require zero setup, and handle highway wind loads. Two 200W panels (400W total) is the sweet spot for most rigs — enough to replenish 1,600–2,000Wh per day. Make sure your generator's solar input can handle the wattage.
 Portable Folding Panels
 100–200W folding panels travel inside the rig and deploy at camp. The advantage: you can angle them directly at the sun and move them throughout the day, getting 20–30% more output than flat roof panels. The downside: setup effort, theft risk, and no charging while driving. Best as a supplement to roof panels.
 Car Charging While Driving
 Every unit on this list charges from a 12V vehicle outlet. At 100–150W typical draw from a cigarette lighter circuit, a 5-hour drive adds roughly 500–750Wh. Some RVers install a dedicated higher-amperage 12V charging circuit from the alternator for 300–500W, cutting charge time significantly.
 Inverter Considerations
 Pure sine wave output matters for RV use. All five picks on this list produce clean pure sine wave AC power, safe for sensitive electronics, CPAP machines, and laptop chargers. Cheaper generators with modified sine wave output can damage sensitive devices over time and produce audible buzzing in fans and chargers.
 Pro tip for roof solar: Park with your RV oriented east-west when possible, so the long side of the roof faces south. This maximizes solar exposure on roof-mounted panels throughout the day. At BLM dispersed sites where you choose your own spot, orientation is free — use it to your advantage.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 How much solar generator capacity do I need for RV boondocking?
 For most RVers, 1,000–2,000Wh handles a typical day of boondocking: running a 12V fridge (40–60W continuous), charging phones and laptops, powering LED lights, and running a water pump intermittently. Full-timers who run a microwave, coffee maker, or rooftop AC will need 3,000Wh+ and should look at the ALLPOWERS R3500 or a dual-unit setup. The rule of thumb: calculate your daily watt-hour draw, add a 20% buffer for inverter losses, and make sure your solar panels can replenish at least 80% of that during daylight hours. Our calculator can run these numbers for your specific rig.
 Can I charge a solar generator while driving my RV?
 Yes, and this is one of the biggest advantages of a portable solar generator for RV use. Every unit on this list supports 12V car/vehicle charging. Most Class C and B motorhomes have a cigarette lighter or auxiliary 12V outlet that provides 100–150W of charging power. At that rate, a 2,000Wh unit gains about 500–700Wh during a 5-hour drive — not a full charge, but a meaningful supplement. Some RVers install a dedicated high-amperage 12V circuit from the alternator to charge faster. If you have roof-mounted solar panels, those work while driving too, giving you two passive charging sources simultaneously.
 Do solar generators work with RV 30-amp shore power plugs?
 Portable solar generators use standard household 120V/15A or 20A outlets, not the TT-30 (30A RV plug) or 14-50 (50A RV plug) connectors used at campgrounds. You cannot plug your RV's shore power cord directly into a portable solar generator. Instead, you run individual appliances from the generator's AC outlets using standard plugs, or wire them into specific circuits. Some RVers install a manual transfer switch to feed the generator's output into their RV's 120V distribution panel, but this requires professional installation. For most boondockers, running appliances directly from the generator's outlets is the simplest and safest approach.
 What size solar panel should I pair with my RV solar generator?
 For RV use, aim for panels that can replenish 50–80% of your daily usage during 4–5 hours of peak sun. A 200W panel produces roughly 800–1,000Wh per day in good conditions. For a 2,000Wh generator, 200–400W of panels (one or two panels) is the sweet spot. Rigid panels mounted to the RV roof are ideal for drive-and-charge convenience, while portable folding panels let you angle toward the sun at camp. The EcoFlow Delta 2 Max accepts up to 500W of solar input, and the BLUETTI AC200L handles up to 1,200W — meaning you can wire multiple panels for faster recharging. Start with one 200W panel and add more if you find yourself running low during extended boondocking trips. For detailed sizing math, try our solar calculator .

 How to Choose the Best Solar Generator for Van Life?
 Picking the right solar generator is less about finding the biggest battery and more about matching capacity, output, weight, and charging speed to how you actually live in your van. Here is the framework I use when evaluating units, plus the van-specific considerations that separate a good purchase from a frustrating one.
 Sizing Your Battery to Real Van Loads
 The most common mistake new van lifers make is buying a battery that is too small or far too large. Start by listing your daily loads and their wattage. A typical weekend setup looks like: 12V fridge at 40 to 60W running about 8 hours per day (with cycling), LED lights at 10W for 5 hours, laptop charging at 60W for 4 hours, and phone charging at 10W. That totals around 600Wh per day, which a 1,000Wh battery handles with margin.
 Full-time van lifers typically need 1,500 to 3,000Wh of capacity to avoid daily recharging stress. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 hit the lower end of that range, while the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 and EcoFlow DELTA Pro cover the upper end. Anything below 500Wh is a weekend-only setup unless paired with reliable alternator charging.
 Battery Chemistry: LiFePO4 vs Lithium-Ion
 LiFePO4 (also called LFP) is the chemistry I recommend for any full-time van build. The cycle life is 4,000 to 6,000 cycles versus 500 to 1,000 for standard lithium-ion, which translates to 10 to 17 years of daily use versus 2 to 3 years. LiFePO4 is also more thermally stable, which matters when your battery lives in a van that hits 110°F in summer and 20°F in winter.
 The trade-off is weight and cost. LiFePO4 batteries weigh about 20% more than equivalent lithium-ion units and cost roughly 30% to 50% more. For weekend warriors, that math does not pencil out. For full-time van lifers, it is the only chemistry that makes long-term sense. Most of the BLUETTI and Jackery v2 units in this roundup use LiFePO4; the smaller kits from MARBERO, ZeroKor, and Apowking use lithium-ion to hit lower price points.
 Solar Input and Roof Space
 Solar input ceiling matters more than battery size once you go full-time. A 1,000Wh battery with a 200W solar input takes 5 to 6 hours to refill from empty in peak sun. A 1,000Wh battery with a 1,000W solar input takes about 1.5 hours with the right panel setup. For vans with limited roof real estate, prioritize higher solar input ceilings like the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 (1,000W max) and the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (1,000W max).
 Standard 100W and 200W portable panels work fine with any unit in this roundup. For permanent roof mounting, look at rigid or semi-flexible panels with 200W to 400W ratings. Our RV solar panel kits guide covers panel selection in detail.
 Weight, Footprint, and Van Mounting
 Every pound matters in a van build. A 99-pound DELTA Pro requires permanent mounting and reduces your payload significantly. A 23.8-pound Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 can move with you. For full-time builds where the unit stays put, weight matters less than capacity. For builds where you want to remove the unit for theft prevention or indoor charging, prioritize weight under 30 pounds.
 Footprint matters too. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 at 17L is the most space-efficient 1kWh unit I tested, fitting in places the larger Jackery and EcoFlow units cannot. Measure your available cabinet or garage space before committing to a unit.
 Charging Speed, Ports, and Smart Features
 Fast charging is more than a convenience. The ability to refill from 0% to 80% in under an hour changes how you think about power. You can top off during lunch at a coffee shop, run a microwave without anxiety, and recover quickly after a cloudy day. The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 (45 min to 80%) and BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (50 min to 80%) are the speed leaders in this roundup.
 Port variety matters for gadget-heavy builds. Pure sine wave AC outlets are essential for sensitive electronics. USB-C PD 60W or 100W ports let you charge laptops directly. Wireless charging pads, while not essential, are a small convenience that adds up over years of use. Smart features like app monitoring and UPS switchover are nice but should not drive the purchase decision on their own.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What size solar generator do I need for van life?
 Most weekend van lifers get by with a 500 to 1000Wh unit. Full-time van lifers typically need 1500 to 3000Wh to avoid daily recharging. Match the capacity to your daily watt-hour consumption plus 20% margin. A fridge (40 to 60W for 8 hours), lights (10W for 5 hours), and a laptop (60W for 4 hours) totals roughly 600Wh per day, so a 1000Wh battery works comfortably.
 How long will a solar generator power a van fridge?
 A 12V fridge drawing 40 to 60W running about 8 hours per day (with compressor cycling) consumes 320 to 480Wh. A 1000Wh battery powers it for about 2 days, a 2000Wh battery for 4 days, and a 3600Wh battery for a full week. Real-world runtime is usually 80% to 90% of these calculations due to inverter losses.
 Are solar generators worth it for van life?
 Yes, for most van lifers. Solar generators are silent, fume-free, low-maintenance, and require no fuel. Compared to gas generators, they cost more upfront but save money long-term. Compared to DIY battery systems, they are plug-and-play with built-in inverters, charge controllers, and safety features. The main trade-off is capacity versus portability.
 Can a solar generator run a mini fridge in a van?
 Yes, almost any solar generator in this roundup can run a 12V mini fridge. The fridge draws 40 to 60W, well within the capacity of even the smallest units. The real question is runtime, not capability. A 300Wh unit runs a fridge for about 5 to 7 hours, while a 1000Wh unit runs it for 2 days.
 How do I charge a solar generator while driving?
 Most solar generators in this roundup support car charging via a 12V cigarette port, but it is slow at about 5% per hour. The faster option is connecting a DC-DC charger between your van alternator and the solar generator input, which charges at 30% to 50% per hour depending on alternator output. Alternator charging is the most efficient way to refill while driving.
 What is the difference between a solar generator and a portable power station?
 Technically, there is no difference. Both terms describe a battery, inverter, and charge controller in a portable case. The solar generator label usually implies a kit including solar panels, while portable power station often refers to the battery unit alone. Functionally, they are identical products.
 Do solar generators work in winter for van life?
 Solar generators work in winter, but solar charging efficiency drops significantly. At latitudes above 40 degrees, winter sun angle and shorter days reduce solar harvest by 30% to 60%. LiFePO4 batteries handle cold better than lithium-ion, but charging below freezing can damage cells. Plan for alternator or shore power charging in winter, with solar as a supplement.
 Final Verdict
 After three months of testing across 12 models, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 remains my top pick for the best solar generators for van life in 2026. The combination of 1,070Wh LiFePO4 capacity, 1,500W output, 23.8-pound weight, and 1-hour emergency charging covers more real-world van scenarios than any other unit I tested. For full-time van lifers with serious power demands, the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 is the long-term investment. For weekend trips and tight budgets, the Apowking 146Wh kit handles overnight CPAP and basic charging without weighing you down.
 Whatever unit you choose, size your battery to your actual daily load, prioritize LiFePO4 chemistry for full-time builds, and match the solar input ceiling to your planned roof array. The best solar generator is the one that fits your van, your power budget, and the way you actually travel.

 How to Choose the Best Solar Generator for Your RV
 Buying a solar generator for RV use is not just about picking the biggest battery. You need to match the generator to your RV class, your appliance load, your solar panel pairing, and your shore-power compatibility. The sections below cover the decisions that matter most.
 Sizing the Generator to Your RV Class
 Different RV classes have very different power profiles. A 16 ft campervan running lights and a 12V fridge needs far less than a 40 ft Class A motorhome with two rooftop ACs and a residential fridge.
 Camper vans and truck campers (under 20 ft): 1,000-1,500Wh and 1,500-2,000W covers lights, fridge, phone charging, and a microwave. The BLUETTI AC180 or Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 fit well.
 Travel trailers and Class C motorhomes (20-30 ft): 2,000-3,000Wh and 2,000-3,600W covers a single rooftop AC plus typical appliance load. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 or Jackery HomePower 3000 fit well.
 Class A motorhomes and large fifth wheels (30 ft+): 3,000Wh or more, ideally expandable to 10kWh+. Two rooftop ACs and residential fridge demand the Anker SOLIX F3000 or BLUETTI Apex 300.
 A quick rule of thumb: 1,000Wh of battery per 1,000W of inverter output covers a weekend of typical use. Add 50% buffer if you plan to run rooftop AC.
 30-Amp vs 50-Amp RV Shore Power Compatibility
 RV shore power plugs come in two main types. A 30-amp plug (NEMA TT-30) is the standard for most travel trailers and smaller motorhomes. A 50-amp plug (NEMA 14-50) is the standard for Class A motorhomes and large fifth wheels, and it carries 120/240V split-phase power.
 If your rig has a 30-amp plug (most common), any solar generator with a built-in 30A outlet will plug straight in. The Jackery HomePower 3000, Anker SOLIX F3000, and BLUETTI Apex 300 all include this. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 and BLUETTI AC180 use standard 120V outlets and require a TT-30 adapter.
 If your rig has a 50-amp plug, you need a power station that outputs 120/240V split-phase or you need to pair two units. The BLUETTI Apex 300 is the only unit in our roundup with built-in 120/240V output.
 Running a Rooftop RV Air Conditioner
 A 13,500 BTU rooftop AC draws roughly 1,200-1,500W running and 2,500-3,500W on compressor startup. To run one for 4 hours, you need at least 5,000-6,000Wh of battery. To run one for 8 hours (overnight in summer), you need 10,000-12,000Wh or shore-power charging during the day.
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 (2,042Wh) runs a 13,500 BTU AC for about 4 hours. The Anker SOLIX F3000 (3,072Wh) extends that to 5-6 hours. The BLUETTI Apex 300 with expansion batteries can run overnight.
 If you camp in mild climates (under 80 F nights), a smaller unit with a 5,000 BTU window AC is more practical. If you camp in summer desert heat, plan on the largest expandable system you can afford.
 Battery Chemistry: LiFePO4 vs NMC Lithium-Ion
 Every pick in our roundup uses LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) chemistry, which is the right choice for RV use. LiFePO4 batteries last 4,000-6,000 cycles before reaching 70-80% capacity. NMC lithium-ion batteries (used in some older or budget units) last 500-1,000 cycles.
 LiFePO4 is also safer. The chemistry is far less prone to thermal runaway, which matters in an enclosed RV during hot summer travel. The trade-off is slightly higher weight per Wh, which is why the larger units weigh 60-90 lbs.
 Solar Panel Pairing (Watts of Panels per kWh)
 A good rule of thumb: pair 400W of solar panels per 1,000Wh of battery. A 2kWh unit like the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 wants 800W of panels (four 200W panels). A 3kWh unit like the Anker SOLIX F3000 wants 1,200W of panels (six 200W panels).
 Undersizing solar panels means your battery never fully refills during a sunny day, which hurts boondocking endurance. Oversizing means you waste panel investment. Our guide to portable solar panels for RVs covers panel selection in detail.
 Charging from the Tow Vehicle / Alternator
 Many RVers want to charge the solar generator while driving. Some units accept alternator input through a dedicated port or via a high-power 12V car adapter. The Anker SOLIX F3000 and BLUETTI Apex 300 accept vehicle charging through their high-voltage input ports.
 Charging from a tow vehicle is slow compared to AC or solar — typically 100-200W of input. That is enough for a partial refill during a 4-hour drive but not a full recharge. Plan on solar or AC charging for full refills.
 Solar Generator vs Gas Generator for RV Use
 Traditional gas generators like the Honda EU2200i or Champion 4500W still have a place in RV life. They are cheaper per watt, they refill in minutes, and they handle 240V split-phase loads without pairing. But they are loud (60-75 dB at full load), they produce fumes, and most campgrounds enforce quiet hours that ban generator use after 10 PM.
 Solar generators are silent (22-30 dB), fume-free, and allowed during quiet hours. The trade-off is higher upfront cost per Wh and longer recharge times. For most modern RV use, a solar generator handles 80-90% of power needs and a small gas generator covers the rare high-draw emergency.
